When global oil prices rise, when supply chains are disrupted, and when costs increase, the impact is not felt first by large corporations or multinationals.

It is felt most immediately by small business owners.

The nasi lemak seller who opens at 5am and sees her ingredient costs rise week by week. The workshop owner managing a growing diesel bill. The family business that has served its community for generations and now faces difficult decisions about staying open.

We see you. This government sees you.

That is why our response is grounded not only in words, but in concrete support:

• RM117 million allocated under the 13th Malaysia Plan for eight targeted MSME programmes

• RM53 million to accelerate digital and AI adoption, ensuring technology remains an enabler, not a barrier

• RM500 million in soft loans for businesses affected by global trade tensions

• RM34.9 billion in concessional SME financing through Bank Negara Malaysia

• RM60 million through MATRADE to support SMEs in expanding into new export markets, including Africa, Central Asia and Latin America

The National Economic Action Council or MTEN, is engaging directly with SMEs to understand the challenges on the ground and to shape a more responsive policy framework. This is not policy developed in isolation. It is policy built through partnership.

MSMEs contribute 39.5 percent of our GDP and employ 8.1 million Malaysians, nearly half of our workforce. When we protect small businesses, we protect the foundations of our economy. When we protect the economy, we safeguard the well-being of our people. When we protect jobs, we protect families. 

Our target under the 13th Malaysia Plan is clear. We aim to increase the share of medium-sized enterprises from 1.6 percent to 5 percent by 2030. This means enabling micro enterprises to grow into confident small businesses, and small businesses to scale into stable medium-sized firms. This is not simply economic policy. It is a long-term investment in national strength and economic resillience.

Malaysia’s economy is not built in boardrooms alone. It is built by the individuals who open before dawn and close after dark. They are the backbone of this nation, and this government stands firmly behind them.

Malaysia’s deep tech founders don’t leave for Singapore because they love the food ... they leave because our financial system starves them.

We keep saying Malaysia wants to be an “Innovation Nation.” But our development banks still behave like it’s the plantation era ... demanding collateral, land titles, and predictable revenue streams. Try pitching them a deep tech startup built on AI, biotech, or climate solutions, and they’ll look at you like you’ve asked them to finance a spaceship to Mars.

Meanwhile, the numbers don’t lie. In 2024, ASEAN early-stage tech funding hit ~$2.8B. Guess where it went? Singapore. By Month 9, 2024, it pulled 68% of deal value. By H1 2025, it controlled a jaw-dropping 92% of Southeast Asia’s tech funding. The rest of ASEAN, including Malaysia, is left to fight for scraps.

This isn’t “bad luck.” It’s policy design.

The U.S. wires innovation into its financial DNA:
- SBIR/STTR grants de-risk early R&D.
- The DOE’s Loan Programs Office has already committed over $100B to scale deep tech infrastructure.
- Strategic incentives like the CHIPS Act crowd in private capital at massive scale.

Singapore runs the same playbook regionally ... sovereign-backed co-investments, fast regulatory sandboxes, and patient capital structures. It funds possibility, not predictability. That’s why every serious ASEAN founder eventually ends up with a Singapore cap table.

And Malaysia? We’re still trying to make deep tech fit into SME loan products.

It’s like forcing a Formula One car onto a kampung road and wondering why it can’t accelerate.

If we don’t fix this, Malaysia will become a Copy-Cat Nation (I believe we already are!) ... importing technology we should have built ourselves, instead of exporting our smartest founders across the Causeway.

The solution isn’t another glossy blueprint or “innovation corridor.” It’s rewiring our financial plumbing:
- Accept IP and patents as collateral.
- Offer milestone-based venture debt with government first-loss guarantees.
- Use government procurement as capital to validate local innovations.
- Anchor sovereign fund-of-funds that actually back deep tech, not just safe bets.
- Build regulatory fast lanes with strict timelines, not endless approval queues.

Financial policy isn’t just about loans and grants. It’s about choosing what future you want to build.

The U.S. and Singapore have already made their choice.

If Malaysia keeps funding predictability, we’ll keep buying other people’s futures.

If we fund possibility, we might just build our own.

The question isn’t “can we afford to?” It’s can we afford not to?

Right now, Singapore is eating our lunch — and we’re the ones paying for the table.

There’s a certain tragic comedy in watching Malaysia roll out its largest budget ever. For 2026, RM421 billion is on the table, with billions earmarked for Bumiputera empowerment; RM2.5 billion in micro-loans, RM5 billion in guaranteed SME financing, RM6 billion for education.

On paper, we’re building a high-income nation. In reality, we’re scaling nasi lemak vendors and government sub-contractors.

Look at the output. The TUBE programme generated RM154 million in sales ... respectable, until you realize much of it sits in basic retail and F&B. Meanwhile, RM1.32 billion in financing to Bumiputera companies translates into just 8.1% of GDP contribution.

So why isn’t the needle moving?

Because we’re misallocating talent.

Take Khairul Aming. An engineer by training ... systems, logistics, chemistry. What is he doing? Bottling sambal. His RM4 million restaurant venture pulled 3,000 bookings in minutes. Commercial genius, no question. But it raises an uncomfortable thought; what if that same brain went into deep tech?

Instead, the ecosystem nudges our brightest toward what gets funded. And funding overwhelmingly favors working capital (stock for kedai runcit) and physical assets (more restaurants).

The numbers don’t lie. Billions go to G1–G4 contractors and F&B ecosystems, while high-tech gets scraps ... RM105 million here, training programs there. In a RM421 billion budget, that’s barely a rounding error.

We celebrate success stories like Khairul Aming. Millionaire, household name. But symbolically, it reflects a policy failure. We’re channeling engineering minds into optimizing chili paste supply chains because that’s where the incentives are.

And the result? A risk-averse ecosystem. Why gamble on AI or semiconductors ... years of R&D, uncertain returns; when you can open a restoran with guaranteed loans? Why build factories when fixing drains pays faster?

We are effectively funding dominance in kopitiams and procurement, while deep tech, AI, and green energy remain someone else’s game.

The Madani government talks about a “paradigm shift.” But until we stop treating restaurateurs as the pinnacle of success, and start pushing engineers to actually engineer; we’ll remain consumers of technology, not creators.

It’s time to stop funding the sambal and start funding the silicon.

Some of the most impactful government programs are the ones we don’t hear much about.

Last week we launched RM50 billion in loan guarantees through Skim Jaminan Pembiayaan Perniagaan (SJPP) and Skim Jaminan Kredit Perumahan (SJKP). Not for a fancy mega-project but for a mechanism that will quietly enable tens of thousands of small businesses and families to access financing they couldn't get otherwise.

The Government doesn't hand out money through these programmes, but we guarantee loans. Banks still lend their own capital. Businesses and homebuyers still repay. Markets still function. But the Government absorbs enough risk—up to 80% for businesses, and up to 120% for housing— so that banks will now lend to people they would have previously turned away.

These are people in our everyday lives: warung owners, gig workers, local product manufacturers, fishermen. Most of them don’t receive pay slips, and have no land titles for collateral. Basic requirements that make them “too risky” for banks, and so they are often marginalized when it comes to financing.
 
And yet, collectively they form a critical driving force of our economy. SMEs employ nearly half of Malaysia's workforce and contribute about 40% of GDP. The informal economy - gig workers, traders, contract workers - have grown exponentially since Covid-19 and continues to expand. Shutting them out of the financial system means hampering a key growth engine.

Every ringgit the Government puts into guarantees unlocks significantly more in actual lending. Businesses invest, hire, grow. Families build equity. Tax revenue increases. The economy expands from the base up, not just the top down.

Since 2009, SJPP has guaranteed RM116 billion in SME financing across 85,000 businesses. Since 2008, SJKP has enabled RM25 billion in home loans for 104,000 first-time buyers. In 2025 alone, 14,000 SMEs received RM14 billion in financing, while 27,000 families got RM7 billion in housing loans. Each loan makes a difference in someone's life, and collectively they create tangible impact to the country. 

Congratulations to Prokhas Sdn Bhd, Syarikat Jaminan Pembiayaan Perniagaan Berhad (SJPP) and SJKP on these achievements, and for continuing the important work of enabling growth through inclusion.

Digital Banks in Malaysia are Losing Money…..

Losses of RM200m–RM600m across Malaysia’s digital banks are often waved away as “startup costs.” Some losses are inevitable. Sloppy ones aren’t.

The issue isn’t digital banking. It’s the way many of these banks are being built.

Too many chase deposits before knowing how to deploy them; cos it’s the easiest to do! Paying up for money that ends up in low-yield assets creates negative carry almost immediately. In reality, deposits aren’t the constraint; capital is. With a RM300m minimum capital requirement post-graduation, every product has to justify the capital it consumes.

It’s interesting to look at what worked elsewhere.

Starling Bank treated capital, not deposits, as the scarce resource. Products were sequenced to recycle capital quickly, not to inflate balance sheets. Growth was slower; but losses were controlled.

Lending strategy matters just as much. Long-tenor, low-margin loans look impressive on paper, but they delay income and trap capital early on. Nubank did the opposite: short-duration, fast-turning credit. Capital moved faster, pricing adjusted sooner, and profitability followed.

Fee income is another blind (and “usually” ignored) spot. Payments, FX spreads, SME subscriptions; none are flashy, but they keep revenue flowing while loan books mature. Monzo leaned heavily on interchange and premium accounts long before lending carried the model.

Then there’s discipline. High customer acquisition costs and scaling loans before risk engines are ready don’t accelerate success! They just defer losses. WeBank built risk and data capabilities first, then scaled. Risk wasn’t a control function; it was the product.

The lesson from the UK, Brazil, and China is consistent: digital banks don’t become profitable quickly. They MUST become profitable predictably.

Malaysia’s next digital banking winner won’t be the fastest to grow.
It will be the one that loses slower, learns faster, and earns earlier!

Monee just pulled off what most #banks dream of.

In just 12 months, their #loanbook has almost doubled. From $3.5B in Q2 2024 to $6.9B in Q2 2025. At the same time, the #NPL 90+ ratio dropped to 1%. Banks usually talk about balancing #growth and credit quality, Monee is simply mastering it.

And here’s the jaw-dropper: they now have over 30 million first-time borrowers. That’s 4 million added in a single quarter. For a region where access to formal credit has always been a massive gap, this isn’t just growth. It’s system-changing. Millions of consumers and #SMEs are finally getting access to loans they couldn’t touch before.

The story isn’t only about ShopeePay either. On-platform #lending is still flying, but off-Shopee loans are quietly exploding. #Malaysia alone has already crossed $1B in outstanding loans. Off-platform SPayLater grew more than 40% in just one quarter and now accounts for over 20% of the market. That’s what expansion looks like.

Traditional banks love to present themselves as the guardians of prudent lending. Yet they’re watching from the sidelines while a tech-born lender doubles its book, keeps NPLs at record lows, and signs up tens of millions of new customers.

This isn’t a #FinTech sideshow anymore. It’s the new lending #infrastructure of #SEA.

And if you’re a traditional bank exec reading this… it should keep you up at night.

In today’s digital economy, trust is built on data.

When SMEs understand and manage their financial information from maintaining accurate records to building a strong credit profile, they gain more than just access to financing & they earn credibility and opportunity.

We’ve seen how visibility can transform small businesses. When lenders and partners can clearly see your financial story, decisions become faster, confidence grows, and new growth doors open.

A few best practices for SMEs to improve their chances of securing financing, capital or loans, SMEs can focus on a few key areas:

✅️ Maintain proper financial records
Keep up-to-date bookkeeping, profit and loss statements, and cash flow records. Even simple, well-organized records give lenders confidence that the business is being managed properly.
💡Adopt a book-keeping solution, accounting software or simply start your e-invoicing adoption

✅️ Separate business and personal finances. Many small business owners mix the 2, which makes it difficult for banks to assess actual business performance. Having a dedicated business bank account helps show a clear financial picture.
💡 Setup your business account with any financial institutions, this will help build your credit credibility

✅️ Understand creditworthiness:
Regularly check and build your company’s credit profile. Pay suppliers and existing loans on time, a positive credit record increases trust with lenders.

OCBC aims to provide social loans to 10,000 women entrepreneurs by 2030, up from 2,000 now

OCBC has set a target of providing social loans to 10,000 women entrepreneurs in four markets by 2030 under its Women Unlimited programme, it said on Wednesday (Sep 17).

This compares to the more than 2,000 women-owned small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the region that had received social loan commitments totalling close to S$600 million as of June.

Launched in Singapore in April 2024, the Women Unlimited programme offers financing of up to S$100,000 for women-led startups within their first two years of incorporation, with processing fees waived.

The initiative was extended to Hong Kong and Malaysia in April and August this year, respectively. In Indonesia, a similar programme called Women Warriors has been in place since 2020.

The loans aim to promote the socioeconomic advancement of women in the economy and strengthen the growth and resilience of women-owned businesses.

In Singapore, loan commitments to women-owned SMEs grew by more than 20 per cent year on year in the first year of the programme. Currently, one in three of OCBC’s SME customers in the four markets are women-owned. In Singapore, the proportion is 36 per cent.

OCBC’s data indicates that women generally take up fewer loans than men, resulting in lower revenue growth in their initial years, said Linus Goh, head of global commercial banking at OCBC, at a media briefing.

Women-owned SMEs in Singapore typically record about 30 per cent lower sales turnover growth in their first three years, compared to SMEs owned by men, the bank’s data showed.

However, those that obtained financing were able to narrow the gap, said Iris Ng, head of emerging business, global commercial banking at OCBC.

#Blockchain | #Tokenization Malaysia’s Big Leap Into Asset Tokenisation : Lessons for India’s #Fintech Playbook. Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) has released a landmark discussion paper on Asset Tokenisation, outlining a co-creation roadmap to safely bring real-world assets (RWAs) on-chain.

Here are the key highlights and what India can take away 👇

🔹 1. From crypto noise to real-world value
BNM draws a clear boundary between speculative crypto assets and real-world asset tokenisation — focusing on tokenised bonds, loans, deposits, and stablecoins denominated in Ringgit.
 
🔹 2. Co-creation over regulation
Instead of a top-down approach, Malaysia is going collaborative and experimental:

Establishing a Digital Asset Innovation Hub (DAIH) — a regulatory sandbox-style ecosystem for pilots.

Creating an Industry Working Group (IWG) to align banks, fintechs, and regulators on standards.

Launching a 3-year roadmap (2025–2027)

This co-creation approach could serve as a template for RBI and SEBI as they evaluate frameworks for tokenisation and digital securities.

🔹 3. Purpose-built innovation — not tokenisation for tokenisation’s sake
BNM emphasizes a value-first lens:
Tokenisation should only be applied where it solves real frictions — like SME financing or settlement delays.
API-based or open finance solutions might sometimes be better than blockchain.
 That’s a level of tech-pragmatism India’s policymakers and startups could emulate.
🔹 4. Early focus on financial instruments, not property deeds
Malaysia starts simple — tokenising well-understood regulated instruments (bonds, deposits, loans) before venturing into complex asset classes like real estate.
 India’s journey could mirror this sequencing: start with regulated instruments under the sandbox before scaling to other sectors.

🔹 5. Guardrails for stability and trust
BNM embeds “compliance by design” into its framework:
“Same activity, same risk, same regulation” — tokenisation doesn’t mean escaping licensing.
Only KYC’d participants can access tokenised platforms.
Focus on tokenised deposits and MYR-backed stablecoins, ensuring “singleness of money” remains intact .

🔹 6. Strategic use case: Tokenised Supply Chain Finance
One standout example:
 BNM proposes tokenising supply chain receivables, allowing SMEs to leverage anchor buyers’ creditworthiness for financing — a challenge India faces too.

 Imagine MSME invoices tokenised on a permissioned blockchain — enabling instant, transparent credit flow via banks or #NBFCs.

🔍 What India can learn

✅ Build a regulator-industry working group like Malaysia’s IWG under RBI’s Innovation Hub.

 ✅ Anchor tokenisation around real-world impact — financing, green assets, trade settlement — not speculation.

 ✅ Design for interoperability and public-private collaboration from day one.

 ✅ Pilot tokenised deposits and government securities as foundational use cases before moving to broader assets.

🔍 Three countries. Three levy models. One shared challenge: building future-ready workforces.

A new comparative study from @SUSS-IAL (Singapore) and the Institute of Asian Studies, Chulalongkorn University (Thailand) does exactly what our VET community needs more of — rigorous, evidence-based cross-country analysis of how skills financing actually works in practice.

👥 The researchers: Dr Soon Joo Gog and Silin Yang (Dr) (IAL Singapore) and Akkanut Wantanasombut (Chulalongkorn University) bring complementary policy, analytics and labour market expertise to a genuinely complex question.

📌 What's the question?
How do Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand use training levies to finance workforce development — and what can ASEAN learn from comparing them?

🇲🇾 Malaysia — Employer-centric levy-grant
✅ 1% payroll levy, claimed back for approved training
✅ Strong employer ownership and compliance
✅ Now expanding to MSMEs and underserved groups via Program Latihan MADANI
⚠️ Risk: short-termism — firms chase claimable courses over strategic skills planning

🇸🇬 Singapore — Universal pooled fund
✅ 0.25% levy, centrally managed by SkillsFuture Singapore
✅ Cross-subsidises SMEs and lower-wage workers
✅ Drives lifelong learning and sectoral transformation
⚠️ Challenge: bridging the gap between national steering and enterprise-level needs

🇹🇭 Thailand — "Train or pay" compliance model
✅ Large employers (100+) must train ≥50% of workforce or pay a penalty
✅ 200% tax deduction incentivises in-house training
⚠️ Risk: tick-box compliance culture; penalty too modest to deter non-training
⚠️ The "missing middle": SMEs largely excluded from the system


💡 What strikes me as a VET practitioner:
🔑 No single model wins. Each reflects a governance philosophy — employer autonomy vs. national steering, inclusivity vs. simplicity, incentive vs. obligation.
🔑 The real differentiator is not the levy rate — it's institutional capacity, quality assurance, and outcome measurement.
🔑 Thailand's experience is a cautionary tale: when the penalty is cheaper than the training, compliance beats transformation.
🔑 Singapore's ecosystem approach — investing in labour market intelligence, adult educator capability, and R&D alongside subsidies — is what turns a levy into a learning system.
🔑 For ASEAN as a whole: the path forward involves regional coordination — shared credentials, joint programmes, and peer learning between systems.

SME business owners in Malaysia actually have multiple funding options, the challenge is knowing which fits your stage and readiness. 

I would like to share a clear breakdown you can use. This isgreat for both strategy and advisory.

Funding options for SMEs in Malaysia

1️⃣ Bank Financing, most common & still the backbone of SME funding and these options available are:
✅️ Term loans (expansion, capex)
✅️ Overdraft (working capital)
✅️ Trade financing (LC, invoice financing)
👉 Best for established SMEs with track record, strong financials, and collateral.

2️⃣ Government Grants & Soft Loans
Lower cost, sometimes partially subsidised but competitive. SME Corp, MIDA, MDEC offer this
✅️ Automation & digitalisation grants
✅️ Industry-specific incentives
✅️ ESG / sustainability funding
👉 Best for SMEs looking to upgrade capabilities, tech adoption, or entering new sectors.

3️⃣ Development Financial Institutions (DFIs) 
✅️ Focused on SME growth and nation-building.
👉 Best for SMEs that may not fully meet commercial bank criteria but have strong business potential.

4️⃣ Alternative Financing (Fast Growing)
More flexible, faster approval but at a higher cost.
✅️ Peer-to-peer (P2P) financing
✅️ Equity crowdfunding (ECF)
✅️ Invoice financing platforms
✅️ Platforms regulated by:
Securities Commission
👉 Best for SMEs needing quick access, startups, or those without strong collateral

5️⃣ Venture Capital & Private Equity
Equity funds where you give up shares, not repay loans
✅️ VC firms
✅️ Corporate venture arms
✅️ Angel investors
👉 Best for high-growth startups, tech-enabled SMEs, scalable models.

6️⃣ Trade Credit & Supplier Financing
Often overlooked but very practical, this include
✅️ Extended payment terms from suppliers
✅️ Distributor financing arrangements
👉 Best for managing cash flow without taking formal loans.

7️⃣ Islamic Financing (Shariah-Compliant) widely available from banks like Maybank Islamic, Bank Islam
✅️ Murabahah (cost-plus financing)
✅️ Tawarruq
✅️ Ijarah (leasing)
👉 Best for SMEs preferring asset-backed, ethical financing structures.

8️⃣ Credit Guarantee Schemes (Easier Loan Approval) from SJPP/CGC
✅️ SMEs without collateral get bank financing.
👉 Banks are more willing to lend because risk is partially guaranteed.

9️⃣ Internal & Hybrid options often combined with external funding.
✅️ Retained earnings
✅️ Shareholder injection
✅️ Strategic partnerships / joint ventures
👉 Best to strengthen financial position before seeking external funding.

How to Choose the right options, consider where your business are:

💡Early stage - Alternative financing, Grants
💡Growing steadily - Bank loans with SJPP/CGC support
💡Scaling aggressively - VC, Private Equity
💡Cash flow- Invoice financing, overdraft

Many business owners think giving an interest-free intercompany loan is a simple internal decision.

And from an operational point of view, it often makes sense. It may be done to support business operations, expansion, or the cash flow needs of another related entity. But from a #TransferPricing perspective, the tax authority may view it very differently.

In a case we came across, a taxpayer provided interest-free intercompany loans and advances to another company where a common director was considered to have control or influence over both entities.

During a tax audit, this was treated as a #RelatedPartyTransactions issue that did not meet the #ArmsLengthPrinciple. As a result, #DeemedInterest was imposed, followed by additional tax, penalty, and surcharge.

The key issue was not whether a company can give an interest-free loan. The issue was whether the arrangement complied with the arm's length principle under Section 140A of the Income Tax Act 1967.

If independent parties would have charged interest, the tax authority may impose a market-based interest rate.

This is where many companies may be caught off guard. In practice, these decisions are often made for commercial or operational reasons. But during a tax audit, the focus shifts to whether there is proper documentation, commercial justification, and support for why no interest was charged.

As businesses grow, internal financing arrangements need to be looked at more carefully from both a commercial and tax perspective.

A useful question to ask is this: 
Would an independent party have agreed to the same arrangement on the same terms?

Transfer pricing is becoming increasingly relevant not just for large multinationals, but also for privately held groups and SMEs in Malaysia.

Credit Scoring - Understanding How Credit Scores Affect You.

Credit scoring is important in consumer credit like mortgages, credit cards, small business loans etc. 

Credit scores impact your lives in a few ways:
1. One of the determinants of approval or rejection of loan 
2. Determines the level of interest rate on loan 
3. When seeking employment, prospective employers usually do a credit check as part of background check, pulling bureau score. Bad scores, bankruptcy status can affect employment. 
4. For SME, small businesses, solopreneurs, you act as a director of your private limited company. Your company's loan repayment pattern may affect your credit score. 

Looking into more detail. 

When you apply for a loan at a bank - like mortgages, credit cards, generally two things a bank would do:
1. Do a Know Your Customer (KYC) check, to establish identity of customer, know customer profile and if anything the bank should be worried about (criminal records etc)
2. Run the credit scoring model and get your internal credit score, which gives an indication of your repayment capability and ultimately approval or rejection of loan.

There are two types of credit scores:
1. Internal credit score, using a bank's own model
2. External credit bureau score, by some approved credit bureau. In Singapore, it is by Credit Bureau Singapore.

Most banks have their own internal credit scoring model. What goes into the model to give its "prediction". 

Firstly, from the information you supply the bank e.g income information, tax declaration, occupation, employment status etc. Demographic info e.g age, race are considered discriminatory in loan approvals.

Secondly, you loan behaviour. Past repayment patterns, prompt or no prompt. You credit card limit utilisation, do you max out the limit and just pay the minimum. This behaviour attributes are collected across all the banks, every loan you have is accessed - through credit bureaus, who collect information across the banking industry. 

The more times you miss payment, the habit of just paying minimum repayment on credit cards generally give worse credit score. 

Then just some colours on external bureau credit score. In Singapore, CBS, or in Malaysia, CCRIS, Credit Bureau Malaysia. These bureau provide a credit score to every individual who has a bank loan, or a neutral score of applicant doesn't have any loan at all. Bureau score generally can be made available upon request, for a fee. And looked up for a variety of reasons, including new employment checks.

Very very generally, if you have no loans - a neutral bureau score, and don't have permanent employment or cash flow income, higher likelihood for not approving loan. Hence a lot of consideration and discussion on financial inclusion, for small businesses and the unbanked. Something digital banking aims to overcome. 


Quick info on credit scoring. 

PS: Credit scoring underlying model can be complex. A mix of statistical algorithms, business intuition etc.

MALAYSIA'S BANKING SECTOR CONFRONTS MOUNTING HEADWINDS

Malaysia's banking industry faces a convergence of structural pressures stemming from recent fiscal policy shifts. Expanded Sales and Services Tax (SST), increasingly significant utility rate hikes and mandatory EPF contributions for foreign workers have compressed corporate margins, particularly among Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs).

Bank Negara Malaysia's latest Financial Stability Review reveals that median cost of goods sold continues to rise steadily, touching 75.4% compared to 74.9% in December 2024. Of more concern is the uptick in SME gross impaired loans which rose from 3.4% in H2 2024 to 3.6% in H1 2025, while the broader corporate sector managed to hold steady at 3.1%. With SMEs accounting for over 20% or RM401.8 billion of banking sector loans and 51% of business lending, this disproportionate deterioration bears closer attention.

The erosion in credit quality coincides with largely decelerating growth dynamics. While system-wide loan growth has continued growing, coming in at 5.4% in August and 5.5% in September 2025, analysts project a contraction to 5.1% by the year’s end, sliding further to 4.6% in 2026. Deposit growth meanwhile remains stagnant at 3.1% - well below historical averages - suggesting generally constrained funding capacities.

While the financial sector as a whole is still in the black, Net Interest Margins (NIMs) and non-interest income remain under pressure across the sector, prompting Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) to lower the Statutory Reserve Requirement by 100 basis points earlier this year in order to bolster overall liquidity. 

Macroeconomic tailwinds have also since weakened, leading BNM to issue a revised 2025 GDP estimate of 4.0-4.8%, down from the earlier 4.5-5.5%. Despite the Ringgit's exceptional yearly performance – especially against ASEAN currencies - equity markets have experienced some RM16.4 billion in foreign outflows through September - a clear signal of investors’ larger read of Malaysia’s country risks.

These challenges precede any meaningful assessment of the impact of U.S. tariffs nor of the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART) signed recently - both of which could materially affect export-oriented corporates and, by extension, the sector’s overall asset quality.

It is increasingly clear that a strategic consolidation of the banking sector must be given serious consideration in the coming months. The efficiencies of scale, diversified portfolios and enhanced capital buffers it would bring will help better position our institutions in navigating existing and coming uncertainties while preserving its larger stability, thus providing an anchor for Malaysia's competitiveness in an increasingly fragmented global economy.

Why Digital Banks in Malaysia Lose Money — and How New Entrants Can Lose Less

Losses of RM200m–RM600m across Malaysia’s digital banks are often brushed off as “normal startup costs.” Some level of loss is unavoidable. Poorly controlled losses are not.

The problem isn’t digital banking. It’s how many of these banks are being built.

Too often, deposits are chased aggressively before there’s a clear way to deploy them. Paying up for money that sits in low-yield assets creates negative carry almost immediately. In reality, capital — not deposits — is the real bottleneck. With a RM300m minimum capital requirement post-graduation, every product has to earn its keep.

Lending strategy matters just as much. Long-tenor, low-margin loans might look like growth, but they weaken the economics early on. Shorter-duration, faster-turning credit allows capital to recycle and income to show up sooner.

Fee income is also underestimated. Payments, SME subscriptions, FX and embedded services may not be exciting, but they provide steady revenue while loan books are still finding their footing.

In the end, survival comes down to discipline — customer acquisition costs and risk management more than anything else. High CAC and scaling loans before the risk engines are ready simply push today’s growth into tomorrow’s losses.

The lesson from markets like the UK is clear: digital banks don’t become profitable quickly — they become profitable predictably.
Malaysia’s next digital banking success won’t be the fastest to grow.
 It will be the one that loses slowly, learns fast, and earns early.

Bangladesh’s capital market remains closed to new issuers despite rising financing costs. While bank lending rates have increased to 14–15% from single digits over the past two years, not a single IPO has been launched since March 2024, even though 66 merchant banks are licensed. In contrast, India hosted over 370 IPOs in a single year. 

Even Norway’s Sovereign Wealth Fund which has stakes in a few Bangladeshi companies through the Norges Bank Investment Management had exited its stakes in Beximco Pharmaceuticals PLC and Singer Bangladesh Ltd mid way through 2025, citing regulatory concerns.

The IPO freeze has persisted for more than 18 months now, following the political transition and the appointment of a new Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission (BSEC). Regulatory data show deep structural weaknesses: 42 out of 66 merchant banks failed to submit a single valid IPO proposal within the two-year requirement under the Public Issue Rules, 2010, while all submitted proposals from others were rejected.

Economists and regulators argue that many merchant banks have moved away from their core mandate of IPO origination and corporate restructuring, focusing instead on proprietary investments, private placements, and short-term financing. This has left an overcrowded but largely inactive intermediary sector. Companies approach the capital market for long term sustained financing and the decision of what the company does with the funds should be catered to its capital management and not tied to how it “can and cannot “ utilise the funds! 

The BSEC says reforms to the Public Issue Rules do not prevent new submissions and has signalled tougher enforcement, alongside updates to the Merchant Banker and Portfolio Manager Rules. Still, industry insiders estimate around Tk1,000 crore in IPO applications were withdrawn or cancelled amid regulatory uncertainty, hurting confidence among issuers and intermediaries.

Regional comparisons are stark. In India, only 25–30 active merchant banks (out of 102) facilitated roughly 373 IPOs and SME listings in 2025, supported by strict accountability frameworks; similar to those in Pakistan, Malaysia, and Thailand.

With equity fundraising stalled, Bangladeshi businesses are increasingly reliant on high-cost bank loans, delaying investment and expansion. Market participants say reviving the primary market will require weeding out inactive licences, faster and more predictable approvals, and greater emphasis on bonds and preference shares, alongside stronger regulatory discipline.

BNM just dropped its discussion paper on asset tokenisation — and it’s a big deal.

I just went through the discussion paper and to me, this is the strongest signal that Malaysia is seriously moving toward regulated tokenised finance.

This isn’t about crypto speculation, it’s about bringing real-world assets (RWA) — bonds, loans, deposits, even sukuk — on-chain, in a way that’s supervised, compliant, and aligned with monetary stability.

A few points to highlight:

1️⃣ 𝐁𝐍𝐌 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐚𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚 𝐜𝐨-𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐚𝐜𝐡.

They’re not rushing into regulation.

Instead, they’re inviting banks and startups to collaborate through the new Digital Asset Innovation Hub (DAIH).

That’s a shift from regulating innovation after it happens, to co-designing it together.

2️⃣ 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐮𝐬𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐦𝐚𝐤𝐞 𝐬𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞.

BNM highlights areas like:
a. supply chain financing for SMEs,
b. tokenised sukuk and bonds,
c. programmable payments and tokenised deposits.

These are areas where tokenisation can actually solve real frictions — not just add “blockchain” for the sake of buzzwords.

3️⃣ 𝐓𝐨𝐤𝐞𝐧𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐲 𝐢𝐬 𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞.

BNM is open to MYR-denominated stablecoins and tokenised deposits issued by licensed banks — so long as they preserve what BNM calls the “singleness of money”.

In simple terms: one token ringgit = one real ringgit.

4️⃣ 𝐁𝐮𝐭 𝐁𝐍𝐌 𝐝𝐫𝐚𝐰𝐬 𝐚 𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐦 𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞.

This paper isn’t an endorsement of crypto trading or unbacked tokens.

The focus is purely on tokenisation that creates real economic value — not speculative hype.

My take?

If you’re in banking, fintech, or capital markets — this is your cue to get involved.

Join the conversation early. Engage through DAIH. Start thinking how your products could be tokenised without losing regulatory clarity.

And for lawyers — this is where things get interesting.

We’ll soon need to define how tokenised instruments achieve legal equivalence with traditional contracts.

This paper could be the start of a new chapter in our financial system.

It's great to see CapBay and CGC Digital launching their new digital guarantee scheme for our MSMEs. Alhamdulillah, a big step forward for financial inclusion in Malaysia.

But this excellent news also creates a vulnerable new ecosystem that we need to talk about.

We're now rapidly connecting thousands of MSMEs that often lack the budget, awareness, or resources for cybersecurity. From my experience, this creates a huge blind spot. These smaller businesses become the perfect pivot point for attackers to get into our larger corporate and financial platforms.

Here are some thoughts from my side:

✅ Let's be realistic—businesses getting RM50k to RM500k in financing don't have dedicated IT security teams. They are the most at risk.

✅ These central digital platforms, while efficient, become high-value targets. A single compromised SME credential could open the door to the whole system.

✅ Budget 2026 focuses on securing critical infrastructure. My view is simple: the SME digital ecosystem is now part of our critical national infrastructure.

✅ In my years as a CISM and one of ASEAN's Top 30 CISOs, I've seen this pattern: the weakest link tends to be the partner with the least resources.

This is not to say innovation isn’t important—it is. What I’m emphasizing is the need to pair it with sound risk management. So here’s an idea: why not establish "cyber resilience guarantees" alongside existing loan guarantees? A public-private effort to give SMEs the basic cyber hygiene support they urgently need.

We must walk the talk. Financial inclusion drives progress, but we can’t afford to wait for a serious breach before addressing this gap.

I welcome insights from fellow leaders in policymaking on this. Should cyber hygiene support be a built-in part of these digital financing initiatives?

State Bank of Pakistan (SBP)'s Paradox: 
Inclusion for Speeches, Exclusion in Practice.

No country can claim genuine economic growth or inclusive social welfare while its citizens are locked out of home ownership. Beyond shelter, owning a home provides family security, community stability, and high-multiplier returns across construction, jobs, and allied industries.

Unfortunately, not in Pakistan. Our mortgage-to-GDP ratio remains abysmal: at around 0.25%, it's among the lowest in South Asia. 

Peer Comparisons: What’s Possible (and What We’re Missing)

Production Landscape
- Annual production: 350,000–400,000 MT

- Key regions: Dodoma, Singida, Manyara, Mbeya, Rukwa, Katavi, Tabora & Simiyu
- Average yield: 0.8–1.2 MT/ha (low due to limited certified seed & mechanization)


Consumption & National Deficit
- National edible oil demand: 650,000 MT/year
- Domestic supply (all oilseeds): 250,000–300,000 MT
- Annual deficit: 350,000–400,000 MT
- Imports: 60% of edible oil needs

Note: Tanzania remains a net importer despite strong agro-ecological potential.

Imports & Exports

Imports
- Import bill: US$250–300+ million annually
- Sunflower oil imports (2023): 7,600 MT (US$9.5M)
- Main suppliers: Malaysia, India, Ukraine, Turkey & Kenya

Exports
- Limited (US$2–5M annually)
- Main markets: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, Uganda & Oman

Sector Growth Opportunities
1. Expansion of cultivated area (Central Corridor)
2. Hybrid seed multiplication & local seed systems
3. Mechanization & irrigation financing
4. Medium/large-scale processing plants
5. By-products: Sunflower cake (strong livestock feed market)
6. Regional trade under AfCFTA & EAC frameworks

Strategic Opportunities for Commercial Banks

A. Upstream (Farm Level)
- Input loans (certified seed + fertilizer bundles)
- Mechanization asset finance
- Outgrower scheme financing (processor-backed)

B. Midstream (Aggregation & Storage)
- Working capital for aggregators
- Warehouse receipt financing
- Structured commodity finance

C. Downstream (Processing & Trade)
- Oil mill/refinery expansion loans
- SME processor financing
- Trade finance for import substitution
- Export finance to EAC & AfCFTA markets


Strategic Recommendations for Commercial Banks
1. Develop a Sunflower Value Chain Financing Model (Farmer → Aggregator → Processor).
2. Structure contract farming models with partial guarantees.
3. Mobilize blended finance via development partners.
4. Bundle crop insurance + production loans.
5. Target women & youth producer clusters.
6. Position as a key financier of edible oil import substitution.

Our people often say the best lessons aren’t taken within the confines of a classroom. They come with age, with living, and with stories told by strangers over an iced coffee in places far from home.

These are the lessons that change you — in ways you never imagined. They shift your thinking, your values, and the very world around you.

At the Ecole de Management du Groupe ISM 
where I’m pursuing my Master’s in International Management (MBA), I feel privileged to have both, the classroom and the world. It’s like having my cake and then getting more cake. 

Last semester, we studied Emerging Markets and Business Development. I explored how countries use small and medium enterprises to transition from agriculture to manufacturing, even designing a business entry strategy for Brazil.

Today was different. For an hour, we learned about Malaysia’s entrepreneurial landscape and how African managers can build better, as Malaysia did.

Throughout that lesson, I felt broken! Broken by the idea that it might take Sierra Leone a hundred years to accomplish what Malaysia did in twenty.

Malaysia, the world’s third-largest producer of palm oil, wasn’t always this way. Palm oil came through British colonization, the same crop Sierra Leone once led in producing. Like us, Malaysia was colonized by Britain, but also by Portugal and Japan. Yet they moved from agriculture to manufacturing, and now toward a fully digital economy, while we remain in a loop, swinging between two parties, some days hopeful, other days not at all.

In the 1980s, Malaysia launched the Look East Policy, learning from Japan, Korea, and Taiwan. They built trade agreements, exchanges, and practical policies that worked.

Meanwhile, Sierra Leone has had multiple development agendas since 2007, yet for the average citizen, little has changed. We spend time drafting hundred-page documents that few read or understand. The line between what’s achievable and what’s not remains blurred.

Our professor today spoke about leadership — vision matched with the willingness to lead change. Start small, he said: fix electricity, water, schools; build partnerships, innovate, expand.

Malaysia also built a strong SME culture. Over 50% of its economy comes from the service sector many led by young people. Entrepreneurship isn’t just taught; it’s supported. There’s even a dedicated SME bank for loans, grants, and mentorship.

In Sierra Leone, while starting a business is easier today, sustaining one isn’t. This isn’t an individual problem, it’s a policy one. The government and private sector must work together to create an ecosystem that supports youth entrepreneurs with both funding and mentorship.

We can do better. We must do better. My hope is that our next president drafts a 20-page (or less) development plan, one every Sierra Leonean can understand, believe in, and rally behind.

OCBC aims to provide social loans to 10,000 women entrepreneurs across Singapore, Malaysia, Hong Kong and Indonesia by 2030 through dedicated programmes targeted at small- and medium-sized enterprises (SME).

The bank is a fifth of its way there. As of June, OCBC claims to have supported over 2,000 women entrepreneurs with total social loan commitments of close to $600 million.

The loans are borne out of the OCBC Women Unlimited Programme, which the bank has rolled out in four markets across the region. OCBC launched the programme in Singapore under the name OCBC Women Entrepreneurs Programme, where women-owned SMEs can secure financing of up to $100,000 within the first two years of incorporation. OCBC has also waived the 1.5% “facility fee” levied on approved loan amounts.

Women entrepreneurs are often “a little bit more cautious at the start”, says Linus Goh, head of global commercial banking at OCBC Bank. This makes them less likely to take up a loan early in their business journeys, he adds at a Sept 17 media briefing.

“Lots of entrepreneurs at the beginning — if things were left to themselves — they raise some capital on their own and will exhaust that capital first before they seek help,” says Goh. “But actually the idea is that you draw on a facility concurrent with your capital, and then you have a credit record that starts to develop early, so that gives you the wherewithal to get started well… The stigma of taking the loan earlier was something that we wanted to remove.”

According to OCBC, loan commitments extended to women-owned SMEs in Singapore grew by more than 20% in the 12 months following the launch of the programme in April 2024. Women-owned SMEs in the food and beverage sector received the highest number of loans, followed by those in the building and construction, and transport and logistics sectors.

Read the new Engine by Starling x EY Malaysia piece on "transaction-led digital banking" this morning. The thesis lands. The case studies don't quite carry it.

Every example is a winner. Starling, Cake by VPBank - Digital Bank, OakNorth, Judo Bank, Superbank, Salt Bank, AMP. Conspicuously absent:

Xinja. Australia's first neobank. Shut December 2020. Modern stack, app-first, well capitalised. Died because it offered 2.25% on deposits with no lending book to match. A GlobalData analyst put it bluntly: any bank paying above-market deposit rates with nothing to deploy them into has a problem. Architecture was not the issue.

Volt. Australia's first online-only bank. Cloud-native, modern core. Shut June 2022 with $113m in deposits after a Series F fell through.

N26. Walked away from 500,000 US customers in January 2022 at a $9bn valuation.

Monzo. Just exited the US in March 2026, twelve weeks after finally getting its EU licence through Ireland. The OCC had rejected its US application back in 2021.

If Gen 4 architecture is the moat, four cloud-native banks shouldn't keep failing on it.

Then there's Starling's own story. The piece doesn't mention that Starling's SME book grew from 87,000 to 330,000 clients in under two years on the back of the UK's Bounce Back Loan Scheme, where it issued £1.57bn of 100% government-guaranteed loans. Lord Agnew called it "a cost-free marketing exercise" in 2022. In May 2025, Starling took a £28.2m provision after voluntarily removing government guarantees on loans where its own fraud checks had been inadequate, plus a £29m FCA fine for "shockingly lax" financial crime controls. Profit fell 26%.

The 9.4% SME share is real. It was also assembled inside a once-in-a-generation policy backdrop and an AML system the regulator found materially deficient. Awkward for a piece selling engineering culture as the moat.
The opening example is also off. An Indian food delivery app extending credit on consumption data is embedded lending, not deposit-led primacy. Two different models, one label.

And the causal chain moves too fast. Good UX, engagement, primacy, cheap deposits, profit. In most markets primacy is still anchored by payroll, mortgage and switching friction. Chime has had scale and engagement for years without either primacy or profitability.

One last thing worth naming: the piece is co-authored by Engine by Starling's CCO, with case studies drawn substantially from Engine by Starling's own customer base. Vendors should make their case. It just reads as a point of view, not neutral analysis.

The argument on cost-to-serve, modularity and segment focus is right. I'd just want it stress-tested against Xinja, Volt, N26 US, Monzo US, and the parts of Starling's own P&L the article quietly left out.

Bank Negara Malaysia - Financial Stability Review October 2025

🔹 Domestic financial markets remained orderly despite global volatility

Despite heightened global volatility, driven by US tariff developments, concerns over global growth and geopolitical tensions, Malaysia’s financial market conditions remained orderly. The Financial Market Stress Index (FMSI) peaked in May but has since moderated, reflecting stabilisation across all asset classes.
The ringgit appreciated by 6.1% against the US dollar between March and September 2025, driven largely by external developments. Malaysia’s favourable economic prospects, ongoing structural reforms and continued engagements with corporates are expected to provide ongoing support for the ringgit.

🔹 Business resilience sustained amid cost pressures

In the first half of 2025, business operations remained resilient, supported by resilient domestic demand and sustained economic activity. However, profitability was constrained by persistent cost pressures, particularly in sectors affected by higher labour and material costs. Despite these challenges, businesses maintained their financial strength. The median interest coverage ratio stood at 6.2 times, while the share of firms-at-risk remained stable at 24.4%.

The credit quality of business loans was sustained, with the impairment ratio unchanged at 3.1%. While a small segment of small and medium enterprises (SMEs) continued to face repayment challenges, signs of financial stress remained contained. The share of SME loans under repayment assistance programmes continued to decline, accounting for 4.1% of total SME loans and just 0.7% of total loans in the banking system and development financial institutions.

Looking ahead, the operating environment is expected to remain challenging in the second half of 2025. Nonetheless, moderating input prices and firms’ ongoing cost management strategies are expected to alleviate some of the pressures. Additionally, strong domestic demand and continued investment activity will remain as key pillars supporting business resilience.

🔹 Household resilience anchored by favourable economic and labour market conditions

While the household debt-to-GDP ratio edged slightly higher to 84.8%, borrowers’ debt-servicing capacity remained healthy, underpinned by banks’ prudent lending standards. Key indicators of debt repayment capacity remained sound, with the median debt service ratio (DSR) at 41% for newly approved loans and 33% for outstanding loans.

Overall, the quality of household borrowings remained sound, with the loan impairment ratio unchanged at 1.1%. The share of household loans under repayment assistance programmes continued to decline, reflecting sustained repayment behaviour. Despite ongoing cost-of-living pressures, signs of financial stress among household borrowers remained limited and contained, with no evidence of widespread deterioration in repayment trends.

So you want authoritative ledgers? Be careful what you wish for.

The Straits Times reports:

"It was the day after April Fool’s, and Mr Elgar Kwek thought the pranks and cruel jokes were behind him.

He opened a letter he had received from the Singapore Land Authority (SLA).

It showed a caveat – a legal document obtained by a potential buyer who wants to exercise an option to buy a property – had been lodged by a credit company against a landed property in Katong he owns with his mother."

Not likely to be an option. 🤔 Does the Straits Times not know that there are many kinds of caveats (which is Latin for beware, as in caveat emptor)?

"Mr Kwek, 49, and his partner, Ms Brenda Chow, were surprised...

Mr Kwek, a freelance violinist, called the credit company and learnt that someone had submitted what was supposed to be his NRIC to obtain a loan."

So the caveat was for the security for the loan. 🙄

"The imposter also submitted a notice of assessment, which may have been forged, stating that he had earned an income of $170,000 in 2025 from two companies registered in his name.

Mr Kwek said he has no links to the companies, one registered in 2023 and the other in 2025.

The credit company told him the identity thief had engaged a law firm to lodge the caveat, and further investigations found that the thief had engaged another law firm to secure from SLA a replacement deed for Mr Kwek’s home."

There are no deeds for registered land. What the identity thief must have applied for is a replacement certificate of title.

"The credit company said the imposter had tried to use the property as collateral to get a $2.9 million loan from the credit company.

“They were just one small step away from getting the $2.9 million loan and I’m very sure they would have run away with that money,” said Mr Kwek."

Indeed, he might have gotten away with it if he had gone straight for registration after getting the replacement certificate of title rather than lodge a caveat. If he had managed to do that, Mr Kwek would have found his home security for the loan extended by the credit company because title registries are authoritative even if the owners never authorised the transaction. One reason why Hong Kong's Land Titles Ordinance, enacted in 2004, has never been brought into operation.

Many title registration systems provide insurance against loss but in Singapore, this is only available if the registry was at fault.

"For now, the caveat has been cancelled and Mr Kwek gets to keep his home."

Easily done for caveats, much harder for registrations. But that's the point of title registration: trade off greater security for the acquirer with lesser security for the owner.

"Checks by The Straits Times revealed that he may not be the only victim." 

Be careful what you wish for. If you think obviously fallible checks in the real world is bad, imagine a blockchain land registry where you are one hack/wrench away from losing your home. 🙄

Reading this update reminded me of a recurring challenge I’ve often seen play out, particularly with SMEs and startups in emerging markets: they are rich in ideas but poor in how those ideas are valued.

Many SMEs actually hold strong IP portfolios with real potential to be monetized. The difficulty, however, is that traditional accounting frameworks rarely recognize these assets. As a result, banks and investors often treat them as invisible, even when they are the true drivers of enterprise value.

This is why the analogy of IP as the dark matter of the global economy deeply resonates. We all know it’s there, shaping outcomes, yet we rarely measure it and even more rarely finance against it.

The WIPO–MIDF pilot in Malaysia is, in my view, a much-needed experiment. I have seen too many African founders whose innovations never scale beyond local markets simply because they could not collateralize their IP. Imagine what becomes possible if this barrier is broken.

But there is also a cultural side to this story that feels equally important. Too often, SMEs treat IP registration as the final goal — a certificate to be framed and displayed. Gone are the days when the narrative should stop at registration. From personal experience, a vast majority of SMEs are now aware of copyright, patents, trademarks, and design rights. What remains largely unknown, however, is how to leverage these rights as collateral for loans and other forms of financing.

As the case of MyB Innovation shows, protection is only the beginning. True value emerges when IP becomes the springboard for commercialization, partnerships, and global scaling. That mindset shift is as critical as any financing pilot.

This is also a clear call to action for policymakers in regions like Africa, where creative industries, agritech, fintech, and medtech are booming. If ASEAN can push the boundaries on IP financing and valuation, there is no reason why Africa cannot take inspiration and adapt similar models to its own realities.

Equally, there is a need for more campaigns and awareness on IP financing, not just IP awareness. The narrative must evolve if we want transformative change for SMEs

Financing Africa’s SMEs through Securitization: Unlocking Capital for Inclusive Growth

This paper examines the potential role of securitization in addressing the persistent financing gap confronting small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Africa. 

Despite SMEs accounting for a substantial share of firms, employment and productive activity across the continent, access to finance remains constrained by structural weaknesses including collateral limitations, information asymmetries, shallow capital markets and weak financial intermediation systems. 

The paper argues that the financing challenge facing African SMEs extends beyond conventional credit shortages and increasingly reflects broader deficiencies in market design and liquidity allocation. 

Securitization, defined as the transformation of illiquid financial assets and future cash flows into tradable securities, is explored as an innovative financing mechanism capable of mobilising broader pools of domestic and international capital. 

The paper examines key channels through which securitization can support SME financing, including receivables securitization, trade finance securitization and future revenue stream securitization. 

Drawing on recent international experiences involving multilateral development institutions and emerging structured finance initiatives, the paper highlights both opportunities and regulatory considerations associated with implementation. 

It concludes that while securitization offers important prospects for expanding SME access to finance and strengthening capital market development, its effectiveness ultimately depends on robust regulatory frameworks, institutional readiness and market credibility.

In United Overseas Bank (Malaysia) Bhd v Tan Chong Whatt & Anor, the Court of Appeal delivered a significant judgment in 2024 on the personal liability of directors who sign bank guarantees as principal debtors, meaning they are treated as if they personally took the loan rather than merely backing someone else's obligation.

The company had been wound up. The directors, who had signed the bank facility agreement as both guarantors and as principal debtors, assumed that the winding up order capped their personal exposure. Section 8(2A) of the Insolvency Act 1967 limits the interest that can be claimed against the company after a winding up order. The directors relied on this as protection against post-winding up interest claims.

The Court of Appeal rejected this position. Section 8(2A) applies to the debtor, meaning the company that has been wound up. A director who has additionally signed as a principal debtor is not a mere surety, meaning not simply a backup payer who steps in only if the company defaults. They have contractually assumed primary liability as if they personally borrowed the money. The statutory cap protecting the company does not extend to them. Their liability for post-winding up interest continues to accumulate until the debt is fully discharged.

The court's reasoning followed the Federal Court in Andrew Lee Siew Ling v United Overseas Bank (Malaysia) Bhd, which had established that guarantors who agree to be principal debtors cannot rely on the surety protection provisions in Sections 92 and 94 of the Contracts Act 1950, because they have taken on more than a surety's role.

Most Malaysian bank facility agreements for SME borrowers include a guarantee and indemnity document containing both a guarantee clause and a principal debtor clause. Directors who sign both without understanding the distinction are assuming personal liability that survives the company's winding up and is not subject to the statutory interest cap.

The structural protections that are available but rarely negotiated include a capped guarantee limiting personal exposure to a specific ringgit amount, a specific facility guarantee limiting scope to a named facility rather than all present and future debts under an all-monies clause, and a release mechanism defining the conditions under which the guarantee is discharged.

None of these protections are automatic. They must be specifically negotiated before signing. Banks will not always agree. But the conversation must happen before the guarantee is signed, not after the company is wound up and the interest continues to run.

Think about the most recent personal guarantee you or someone in your network signed for a company bank facility. Was the principal debtor clause specifically explained before signing? YES or NO in the comments. I read every reply.

• Malaysia’s MSMEs Are Stuck in Survival Mode

The OECD’s 2026 SME Scoreboard, which includes Malaysia in a 48 country comparison and a dedicated country snapshot, shows a financing environment that is still tight, expensive, and biased toward survival rather than investment (p. 5, p. 10, p. 143 to 144).  

The numbers are hard to ignore. Across the scoreboard, 34 out of 39 countries still had SME borrowing costs above pre pandemic levels, 10 out of 17 countries showed a higher share of SMEs requiring collateral, and new SME lending only recovered 5.7% in 2024 after a 9% decline in 2023. Even then, lending was still 4% below 2022, while long term SME loans edged down again (p. 18 to 19, p. 24 to 28).  

That is the pressure point for Malaysia. When credit is expensive and short dated, MSMEs stay trapped in working capital mode. They delay equipment upgrades, digitisation, expansion, and the hiring of stronger talent. Inference: that is how stagnant wages become structural, not cyclical, because firms are financing survival instead of capability building. The report does not measure Malaysian wages directly, but it clearly shows the financing pattern that keeps wage growth weak (p. 18 to 19, p. 24 to 28).  

The rest of the data points in the same direction. Factoring fell 3% in 2024 and leasing rose only 1.6%, so alternative finance is still too shallow to change the capital base of small firms. Venture capital recovered in 18 out of 30 countries, but the rebound was uneven and concentrated in a few large artificial intelligence deals. At the same time, fintech driven finance and non bank lenders are becoming more important, which means the market is changing, but not yet enough to solve the core constraint (p. 18 to 19).  

The solution is not more credit in name. It is better credit architecture. The OECD points to asset based finance, leasing, factoring, government guarantees, direct lending, digital invoice registries, and AI enabled underwriting as practical tools to widen access and move firms from survival credit to investment credit. It also calls for better data on loan stock and flow, collateral, fees, gender ownership, and geography, because weak measurement leads to weak policy (p. 14 to 16, p. 18 to 19, p. 27 to 28).  

For Malaysia, If MSMEs remain undercapitalised, productivity will stay weak, wages will stay sticky, and talent will keep flowing toward firms or countries that can pay for capability. The real reform target is not more rhetoric around SME support. It is a shift from survival credit to investment credit, and from low productivity competition to high productivity competition (p. 18 to 19, p. 24 to 28).

With COP 30 begins today in Belém, Brazil, global attention turns to how this COP will shift from pledges to delivery.

At the Climate Governance Malaysia Global Summit 2025, we heard directly from Bruna Cerqueira - Action Agenda Coordinator for the COP 30 Presidency; her message was clear: this COP will be collectively built, “in the spirit of Mutirão” (Brazilian for working together).

What to Expect from COP Belém
📌 Implementation first: Six axes: Energy, Nature, Agriculture, Cities, Social Development anchored by finance + technology + capacity building.

📌 Stable frameworks: ~400 existing initiatives consolidated into 30 objectives, forming activation groups for collective delivery.

📌 Finance as enabler: A new Finance Ministers’ Circle aims to turn the USD 1.3 trillion finance roadmap into real investment flows through de-risking and blended finance.

📌 Nature and equity at the centre: Brazil’s Tropical Forests Forever Fund (TFFF) rewards forest stewardship, restoration, and indigenous participation through an investment-based model.

📌 From rules to real impact: Policies must connect to communities and SMEs-the people’s COP in practice.

My Reflection - Through a Banker’s Lens

What resonates most is the pivot from policy to practicality.

This COP invites financiers, corporates and regulators to turn intent into bankable pathways.

1️⃣ Implementation generates implementation.
Pilot → prove → scale. Banks must design risk-sharing structures that attract first movers; once projects prove cashflow, mainstream capital follows.

2️⃣Adaptation is credit protection.
Climate resilience isn’t philanthropy: it protects repayment capacity. Embedding climate scenarios into risk and pricing models will future-proof portfolios, especially for SME supply chains.

3️⃣ Nature as a financial asset class.
Nature-based solutions can underwrite performance-linked loans and guarantees. Frameworks like CCPT already guide Malaysian bankers, hence the next step is to translate biodiversity services into economic value with credible MRV (Measurement-Reporting-Verification) models.

4️⃣ South-South innovation and learning.
Brazil’s revolving fund model and community custodianship mirror Malaysia’s inclusive transition finance goals. Blending public capital, DFIs and local bank expertise can unlock scale.

5️⃣ Bring the “blockers.”
Bruna was clear: don’t come only with aspirations, come with solutions. Let’s table real bottlenecks - data gaps, permits, FX risk, PPA bankability, so COP can help shape enabling conditions.

As COP Belém begins, let’s move from commitments to capital flow.

In last week’s post, I spoke about tariffs and why diversification is critical. But diversification isn’t just about new buyers—it’s about meeting new standards. Europe, advanced APAC, and Middle Eastern economies are raising the bar on sustainability, labour practices, and ESG compliance. This is where green financing steps in as a strategic enabler of resilience.

What Exactly Is Green Financing?

At its core, green financing channels capital into projects and businesses that drive sustainability. For enterprises, it’s more than funding—it’s a passport into global markets.

Key forms relevant for exporters and manufacturers:

🌱 Green Loans – Loans for renewable energy, wastewater, or energy-efficient equipment. ASEAN and Indian banks are scaling these, often at preferential rates.
💵 Green Bonds – Debt instruments for climate-positive projects. Popular with corporates in India, Singapore, and Malaysia to raise capital for sustainable manufacturing, logistics, or energy transition.
📈 Sustainability-Linked Loans (SLLs) – Flexible credit tied to company-wide ESG performance. Rates adjust to targets (e.g., carbon reduction, supply chain audits, diversity). Ideal for SMEs in ASEAN and India needing working capital and ESG credibility.

Musharaka is a joint venture structure where two or more parties invest capital and share profits and losses based on agreed terms and Shariah Standarts in priority.
Musharaka al-Mutanaqisa allows one partner (the client) to gradually purchase the bank’s share in an asset, ultimately becoming the sole owner. This model is especially suitable for real estate, home financing, and SME development.

Globally, Musharaka-based financing has been adopted in countries such as the UK, Malaysia, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE—providing Sharia-compliant solutions in housing, infrastructure, and business financing.

Uzbekistan now stands at a key moment for Islamic Finance development. With increasing public interest, supportive regulatory movements, and an ideal geographic location, the country is well-positioned to introduce and scale products based on Islamic financial principles. Musharaka al-Mutanaqisa, in particular, holds promise for ethical home financing and inclusive SME growth.

Rental income is another area that requires careful attention. 🟢 In today’s profit-driven world, the concept of interest-free lending feels almost impossible — yet Islamic finance has preserved it for centuries under one timeless principle: Qard Hasan (قرض حسن) — the benevolent loan.

It’s not about profit.
It’s about purpose.
It’s where finance meets faith, and money becomes a means of mercy. 🌙✨

🌿 1️⃣ What Is Qard Hasan? — “A Loan for the Sake of Allah”

💡 Principle:
A Qard Hasan is an interest-free loan extended out of goodwill to help someone in need or to support ethical, productive ventures.
The borrower is required to repay only the principal, with no additional return — and any voluntary gesture (without prior condition) is considered a reward, not riba.

✅ How It Works:
1️⃣ The lender provides funds to support personal or business needs.
2️⃣ The borrower repays the same amount after a defined period.
3️⃣ No interest, no exploitation, no uncertainty.
4️⃣ If the borrower faces hardship, repayment can be extended or forgiven.

⚙️ Example:
🔹 A small entrepreneur receives $10,000 as a Qard Hasan to start a tailoring business.
🔹 After one year, she repays $10,000.
🔹 If she adds $500 voluntarily in gratitude, it’s an act of goodwill — not an obligation.

💼 2️⃣ Applications of Qard Hasan in Modern Finance
Qard Hasan is not limited to charity — it’s an empowerment tool used by Islamic banks, governments, and NGOs for financial inclusion and community development.

💠 Used For:
🔹 Microfinance and SME empowerment
🔹 Student and education funding
🔹 Emergency and social welfare loans
🔹 Support for startups and ethical entrepreneurship

💠 Institutional Examples:
🏦 Islamic banks like Al Baraka, Meezan, and Bank Islam offer Qard Hasan-based microloans.
💡 Zakat and Waqf institutions use it to empower underprivileged individuals to become self-reliant.

⚖️ 3️⃣ Qard Hasan vs Conventional Loan

🟠 Conventional Loan: -	Profit generation,	Interest (Riba), Commercial, Rigid repayment, 	Debt burden

🟢 Islamic Qard Hasan: Social & ethical support, 	Principal only, Benevolence (Ihsan), Can defer or forgive, 	Empowerment

🌙 4️⃣ Qard Hasan in Trade & Development
Qard Hasan isn’t charity — it’s productive compassion.
When embedded in trade finance, it supports:
🔹 Producers during cash flow shortages
🔹 Farmers between harvest cycles
🔹 Exporters facing shipment delays
🔹 Women entrepreneurs and youth ventures

It builds an economy where trust replaces interest, and mutual uplift replaces exploitation.

What Is Slow Capital and Why Does It Matter?

Slow capital is patient, structured, and long-term in nature. It prioritizes business fundamentals and stakeholder alignment over short-term returns. Why Interest Schemes Fit This Mold Perfectly

Under the Interest Schemes Act 2016, businesses can raise funds from the public for commercial activities without issuing shares or taking loans. Instead, they offer interest units, backed by clear contractual obligations and monitored by a licensed trustee and regulator (Companies Commission of Malaysia – SSM).

These schemes:

a. Allow for longer tenures between 5 to 9 years, giving SMEs the breathing space to grow steadily

b. Are governed by detailed trust structures, enhancing investor protection

c. Empower SMEs to retain ownership and control while raising growth-aligned capital

d. Suit asset-backed or recurring revenue models such as property projects, education, lifestyle clubs, and technology platforms

🔹 KLIBOR is Being Phased Out — Introducing MYOR & MYOR-i

A closer look at Malaysia’s new transaction-based benchmarks 👇

💡 Malaysia to Retire KLIBOR by 2029 — Transition to MYOR and MYOR-i

Bank Negara Malaysia will phase out KLIBOR (Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate) by January 1, 2029, replacing it with MYOR (Malaysia Overnight Rate) and MYOR-i — transaction-based benchmarks reflecting actual overnight interbank trades.

📘 What They Are
	•	KLIBOR: Historically, the reference rate banks used to lend to each other and price loans, bonds, and derivatives. It was based on estimates submitted by selected banks, even if no trades occurred.
	•	MYOR: Calculated from actual overnight interbank lending transactions, making the rate more accurate, transparent, and reliable for conventional banking products.
	•	MYOR-i: The Islamic finance equivalent of MYOR. It reflects actual Shariah-compliant overnight interbank transactions, providing a benchmark for Islamic loans, sukuk, and financing products while adhering to Shariah principles.

Why this matters:
	1.	Accuracy & Reliability – reflects real market activity, harder to manipulate.
	2.	Transparency – verifiable by market participants and regulators.
	3.	Risk Management – helps banks and businesses predict borrowing costs.
	4.	Global Alignment – consistent with international benchmarks like SOFR (US) and SONIA (UK).

Analogy:
	•	KLIBOR = “I think I can lend at 3.5% today.” (estimate)
	•	MYOR = “Banks actually lent at 3.45% today.” (fact-based)
	•	MYOR-i = “Islamic banks actually lent at 3.45% via Shariah-compliant methods today.” (fact-based, Shariah-compliant)

💥 Who Will Be Impacted

🏦 Banks & Financial Institutions – corporate, SME, and institutional clients with KLIBOR-linked loans, bonds, and derivatives need updated pricing models, systems, and contracts.
🏢 Corporates & SMEs – review financing agreements and fallback clauses.
💰 Islamic Banks – migrate to MYOR-i for Shariah-compliant products.
📊 Investors & Fund Managers – adjust valuations for sukuk, bonds, and derivatives.

👥 Retail Customers – not directly affected, as personal loans use Base Rate (BR) or Base Lending Rate (BLR), but benefit indirectly from a more stable, transparent financial system.

This transition is more than a rate change — it’s part of modernizing Malaysia’s financial infrastructure for a transparent, data-driven, and globally aligned future.

Modernization, automation, and digital transformation require capital. Financing allows businesses to upgrade without affecting operational cash.

5. Build Business Creditworthiness
Timely repayment of business loans helps establish a strong credit profile, making future financing easier and potentially more affordable.

6. Leverage Opportunities
Bulk purchase discounts, strategic acquisitions, new contracts, and expansion opportunities often require immediate funding. Lending provides the flexibility to seize these opportunities.

7. Maintain Ownership Control
Unlike raising equity, loans allow business owners to access capital while retaining full ownership and decision-making authority.

The objective should not be borrowing more, but borrowing smartly. The right loan structure, tenure, repayment schedule, and lender can significantly impact business profitability and growth.

Businesses don't fail because they borrow; they often struggle because they miss growth opportunities due to lack of timely funding.

Access to credit can help MSMEs expand operations, manage seasonal demand, and stabilise cash flow. However, the true cost of borrowing extends far beyond the advertised interest rate and EMI. Many additional charges and structural terms quietly increase the effective repayment burden. Understanding these factors is essential to protecting working capital, profitability, and long-term creditworthiness.

Here are the 8 Hidden Costs MSMEs Often Overlook:

• Processing fees and upfront deductions that reduce the actual capital received
 • Documentation, legal, valuation, and collateral-related expenses
 • Prepayment and foreclosure charges, including lock-in clauses
 • Penal interest, late payment fees, and EMI bounce charges
 • Bundled insurance and optional add-ons added to the principal
 • GST at 18% on service-related loan charges
 • Flat-rate interest structures that increase effective repayment
 • Opportunity cost of over-borrowing and paying interest on unused capital

Hidden costs do not necessarily imply unfair practices. Most are disclosed in loan documents. The real challenge arises when these terms are not examined closely before signing. To ensure smarter and safer borrowing, MSMEs must: 

• Review the sanction letter thoroughly before acceptance
• Request a complete written breakup of all fees and taxes
• Compare total repayment amount, not just the EMI
• Examine whether the loan follows a flat or reducing balance method
• Assess prepayment flexibility and foreclosure conditions
• Align EMI schedules with business cash flow cycles
• Maintain a repayment buffer to avoid penalties
• Borrow strictly based on actual business requirements
• Monitor the business credit profile periodically
• Choose RBI-regulated institutions that follow transparent lending practices

Responsible borrowing is not about avoiding credit. It is about understanding the full cost before committing. When evaluated carefully, credit becomes a strategic growth tool rather than a financial burden.
