📊 Malaysia’s credit cycle: What the latest trend is really signalling

Loan growth started the year strongly in Q1, but forward-looking indicators now point to a gradual easing of momentum in the months ahead. While this may look like a simple slowdown in lending, I see it reflecting a broader, healthier shift in borrowing behaviour.

🧠 Understanding the signal
Moderating credit growth isn’t just a banking metric—it mirrors economic behaviour, risk appetite, and confidence. Typically, it suggests:

· More selective business expansion
· Greater focus on cash flow and balance sheet strength
· Reduced reliance on leverage
· More disciplined risk-taking among corporates and SMEs

This phase doesn’t automatically mean economic weakness. It often marks a mid-cycle normalisation, especially after periods of stronger growth and tighter financial conditions.

🌏 Malaysia in the ASEAN context
Credit cycles vary across the region:
🇲🇾 Malaysia – moderate growth with early signs of cooling; a shift toward quality-focused lending
🇮🇩 Indonesia – still expanding, supported by domestic consumption
🇻🇳 Vietnam – higher growth but more cyclical
🇸🇬 Singapore – structurally stable, less credit-driven
🇹🇭 Thailand – slower credit growth amid softer domestic demand

Malaysia appears to be transitioning earlier than some peers into a more balanced, disciplined phase.

🏦 How banks typically respond
In this environment, banks tend to:

· Gradually tighten underwriting standards
· Prioritise asset quality over loan volume
· Build stronger credit risk buffers
· Favour sustainable borrowers over aggressive expansion

These are standard adjustments that support long-term stability.

📉 What it means for the economy, businesses & consumers
Economy: slower expansion but more efficient capital allocation, reduced overheating risks.
Businesses: more selective financing access, advantage for strong cash-flow companies, phased expansion plans.
Consumers: cautious borrowing, stricter loan approvals, slower household debt growth—but gradual improvement in financial resilience.

⚖️ Final take: where Malaysia is heading
We’re not in a credit boom, nor entering a contraction. The direction is best described as a gradual transition toward a more disciplined, quality-focused credit environment. It’s a mid-cycle normalisation where credit continues to grow, but with fewer excesses and stronger risk controls. The trajectory points to stability with moderation—healthier long-term conditions, even if momentum feels slower compared to peak cycles.

Over the past couple of years, we have seen a very noticeable shift in the SME lending world.

Lenders are no longer simply relying on statutory accounts that may already be 9–18 months old by the time they are reviewed. Increasingly, they want to understand what is happening in a business today.

Current management information (MI) is becoming a far more important part of the underwriting and credit review process for SMEs.

When we talk about management accounts or management information, this can include items such as:

• Monthly or quarterly profit & loss statements
• Balance sheets
• Cash flow reports and forecasts
• Bank statements
• VAT returns
• Sales trends and pipeline activity
• Aged debtors and creditors
• Commentary around trading performance and current business conditions

Many SMEs are not always best served by relying solely on year end external accounting support. Having some level of ongoing financial oversight, management accounting support, or outsourced finance assistance can make a significant difference, not only in helping business owners better manage performance, but also in strengthening a funding case.

Good quality MI can help demonstrate current trading strength, cash flow position, and importantly, a business’s ability to comfortably service debt. In many cases, it is the recent improved business story and current trading performance that helps get a deal over the line.

One thing that still surprises me, however, is how difficult it can sometimes be for businesses to quickly provide this type of information when requested by lenders. Delays in producing MI, incomplete information, or simply not having visibility on the numbers can slow deals down considerably and sometimes kill opportunities altogether.

At Pathway Commercial Finance, we are seeing lenders place increasing emphasis on visibility, cash flow management, and current affordability when assessing SME funding proposals.

Strong MI shows organisation, control, and direction. If a business is improving, growing, or stabilising, it is far better to be prepared and able to clearly demonstrate that story upfront.

CGTMSE – A Pain or a Gain?

Many entrepreneurs consider CGTMSE the best funding option because it is collateral-free.

But is "unsecured" always the best choice?

CGTMSE was created to support deserving MSMEs, especially first-generation entrepreneurs, manufacturers, and growing businesses that have strong potential but lack sufficient collateral to obtain bank finance.

It is an excellent scheme when used for its intended purpose.

However, today many borrowers opt for CGTMSE simply to avoid offering collateral, even when they possess adequate security. Before making that decision, it is important to understand the actual cost.

What Most Borrowers Overlook
✅ Higher interest rates compared to secured loans
✅ Initial CGTMSE guarantee fees in addition to bank processing charges
✅ Annual guarantee service fees throughout the loan tenure
✅ Higher overall cost of borrowing over the long term

In many cases, CGTMSE-backed facilities may also offer less flexibility when it comes to temporary overdrafts, ad-hoc limits, or special credit accommodations compared to well-secured accounts.

The Right Question

Don't ask:
"Can I get a CGTMSE loan?"

Ask:
"Is CGTMSE the right funding structure for my business?"

If you genuinely lack collateral, CGTMSE can be a game-changing opportunity.

But if quality collateral is available, a secured facility may provide lower interest costs, better banking flexibility, and stronger long-term funding support.

Final Thought
CGTMSE is neither a pain nor a gain by itself.

It is simply a financial tool.

The key is choosing the funding product that best supports your business growth—not just the one that avoids collateral.

Smart entrepreneurs compare the total cost of funds, not just the security requirement.

How SME Loans Quietly Deteriorate Before Becoming “Non-Performing” (Malaysia Context)

SME loan defaults rarely happen overnight.
In most cases, observable liquidity deterioration begins 3–6 months prior to missed instalments
The signals are often behavioural and working capital driven rather than headline profitability declines.

1)  Overdraft is persistently maxed out. 💣 
- OD utilization is constantly > 90%. 
- Repeated excess beyond temporary seasonality. 
- Frequent limit breaches. 
> This signals a cash deficit and becomes a permanent funding rather than a cushion or bridge for cash flow. 

2) Deterioration in Cash Conversion Cycle. 💸 
- Debtor days (DSO) extending without revenue growth. 
- Inventory days (DIO) increasing despite flat sales. 
- Creditor days (DPO) stretching beyond historical norms.
> This signals a possible liquidity stress in balance sheet movements before it manifests in P&L erosion. 

3) Maturity mismatch in facility utilisation. ❌ 
- Short term facilities used to fund CAPEX.
- Continuous and persistent rollover of trade lines. 
- Increasing reliance on ad-hoc temporary facilities.
> This introduces a duration mismatch risk of which will further stress out liquidity.

4) Behavioral shifts.😨 
- Delayed submission of financial information.
- Sudden requests for extension or temporary relief.
- Avoidance of discussions are often early indicators of financial strain.
> Behavorial shifts often precede financial disclosure deterioration. 

Early identification enables proactive intervention by facility resizing, collateral enhancement, or restructuring before the occurrence of full impairment. By the time the first instalment is missed, the deterioration has typically been compounding beneath the surface.

(Valuation) Boss, RM5 Million Sales Does Not Mean Your Company Is Worth RM5 Million

Last week, I asked one SME boss a simple question.
“Boss, how much do you think your company is worth?”

He answered very confidently.

“Mr Koh, last year sales RM5 million. So company value should be around RM5million lah.”

I smiled. This is where many SME bosses get valuation wrong.

Sales RM5million does not mean company value RM5 million.

A buyer does not pay you because your sales look big.
A buyer pays for profit.
A buyer pays for cash flow.
A buyer pays for systems.
A buyer pays for customers that can stay.
A buyer pays for a business that can still run after the boss walks out.

This is the painful part.

To the boss, the company is his baby.
30 years of hard work.
Sunday also work.
Public holiday also answer customer call.
Bank loan, supplier pressure, staff problem, customer problem, IRB letter, everything also he handles.

So when someone says the company may not be worth what he thinks, he feels hurt.

But valuation is not based on feeling.

A company with RM5 million sales but only 2% net margin may be less attractive than a smaller company with RM3 million sales and strong recurring profit.

Revenue is nice for storytelling.
Profit is nicer for valuation.
Cash flow is even nicer.
And clean documentation is the most beautiful.

Many SME bosses also think audited accounts already equal valuation.
No.
Audited accounts answer one question : “Are the financial statements fairly presented?”

Valuation asks another question : “What will a serious buyer actually pay for this business?”

Very different question.
Because a buyer will ask:

Are the profits sustainable?
Are customers too dependent on the founder?
Are personal expenses mixed inside the company?
Are directors’ salaries at market rate?
Are related party transactions properly recorded?
Can the business continue without the boss sitting in office every day?

If the answer is no, the value will be discounted.
Sometimes very heavily.

Now valuation is no longer only for selling business.
It matters for Capital Gains Tax on unlisted shares.
It matters for stamp duty on share transfers.
It matters for succession planning.
It matters when shareholders want to exit.
It matters when family business passes to the next generation.
It matters when IRB asks, “How did you arrive at this value?”

The biggest mistake?

Many SME owners only think about valuation when someone wants to buy their company.

By then, too late already.

Value is built years before the sale.
Clean accounts.
Less boss dependency.
Better margins.
Good systems.
Clear documents.
Proper governance.

All these boring things make buyers pay better.

So boss, don’t wait until someone offers you a low price, then only get angry and say : “Why my business so cheap?”

PS : Authored by Mr Koh Teck Peng, Chartered Accountant, Malaysia and Member of IACV (International Association of Certified Valuators).

Navigating Thailand’s Economic Crossroads Amid U.S. Reciprocal Tariffs.

The recent implementation of Reciprocal Tariffs by the United States, aimed at ensuring trade parity, has placed Thailand under a 19% tariff rate — comparable to Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Cambodia, while Vietnam faces a slightly higher rate of 20%. Unlike traditional tariffs designed primarily for revenue generation, this measure serves as a strategic negotiation tool to press trading partners toward fairer market access.

Attending the seminar “Trump Tariffs: Thailand’s Economic Crossroads Post-Negotiation” provided valuable insights into the geopolitical and economic dynamics shaping global trade. From this perspective, Thailand’s response to this shifting trade environment requires a systematic, three-phase approach:

𝗦𝗵𝗼𝗿𝘁-𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺: Mitigation and Economic Stabilization
The immediate priority should be mitigating the shock from global trade disruptions. Businesses must optimize production and supply chains, leveraging technology to cut costs. At the same time, the government should support vulnerable sectors through targeted tax measures, low-interest loans for SMEs, tax incentives to sustain employment, and strategic efforts to attract foreign direct investment (FDI) — an area where Thailand’s comparatively moderate tariff rate could serve as a competitive advantage.

𝗠𝗲𝗱𝗶𝘂𝗺-𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺: Structural Adjustment and Capacity Building
To reduce vulnerability, Thailand must diversify its economy and strengthen its global competitiveness. This includes expanding export reach to high-growth regions such as South Asia, Africa, and Middle East, while supporting SMEs with financial liquidity, market entry facilitation, and platforms for reskilling and upskilling workers in digital and high-tech industries. These steps would build a more resilient economic base capable of withstanding future disruptions.

𝗟𝗼𝗻𝗴-𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺: Innovation-Driven Transformation
Thailand must evolve from a contract-driven manufacturer to an innovation-driven economy capable of setting trends and standards in global markets. This transformation will require significant investment in education and workforce development in fields such as AI, STEM, and advanced manufacturing, alongside increased funding for R&D collaborations between the private sector and academia. Furthermore, aligning with global environmental and sustainability standards — including carbon reduction, renewable energy adoption, and supply-chain traceability — will be critical for maintaining market access and global credibility.

By pursuing this three-phase strategy, Thailand can move beyond merely weathering the current trade turbulence to laying a resilient, innovation-driven foundation for long-term growth and competitiveness.

	•	Your income should comfortably support the proposed loan repayment after your living expenses and existing obligations.

	•	A positive borrowing and repayment record strengthens your application.

	•	Your employer may need to be on the bank’s approved scheme list or have an existing payroll arrangement with the bank.

	•	National ID

When does a borrower's past stop defining their future?

The conversation around credit history in Nigeria often centres on the consequences of default. But what we rarely discuss at the policy level is the pathway back.

A credit bureau system that only records failure without providing structured rehabilitation does two things: it creates a permanent underclass of excluded enterprises, and it reduces the total pool of bankable businesses in an economy that desperately needs growth.

Here's what concerns me most.

The current system assumes that time alone heals credit wounds. But SMEs operating in our macroeconomic environment face shocks that are often systemic — forex volatility, input cost inflation, or supply chain disruptions that have nothing to do with management competence.

Yet their credit records treat all defaults as equal moral failures.

Progressive credit history frameworks in other markets include provisions for: graduated rehabilitation timelines based on debt clearance milestones, distinctions between economic-driven and willful defaults, and formal mechanisms for rebuilding creditworthiness through supervised lending windows.

We need these conversations at the regulatory table.

The Central Bank's guidelines on credit reporting are comprehensive on capture and retention. But they're almost silent on restoration and reintegration.

This isn't just about fairness. It's about economic efficiency.

Every viable business locked out of formal finance either migrates to predatory informal channels or shuts down entirely. Both outcomes shrink our tax base, reduce employment, and weaken the financial system's reach.

If we're serious about deepening financial inclusion and supporting Nigeria's real economy, we need credit systems that are designed for resilience, not just compliance.

Common Question: What will business finance cost?

What’s the interest rate?
Rates vary depending on:
• Risk profile
• Security available
• Term length
• Type of facility

But the headline rate alone doesn’t tell you the full story.

Are there arrangement or early repayment fees?
Some facilities include:
• Arrangement fees
• Documentation fees
• Early settlement charges

Others build costs into the structure.

Understanding fee mechanics is critical to comparing options accurately.

Is it fixed or variable?
• Fixed rates give certainty and predictable repayments.
• Variable rates may track base rate movements and offer flexibility.
The right choice depends on your appetite for risk and market conditions.

What’s the total repayable amount?
This is the number that matters.
Look at:
• Total cost of capital
• Monthly impact on cashflow
• Return generated from using the funds

The key question is:
“Will this generate a return greater than the cost?”

Chinese SMEs expand into ASEAN through digital-first model

Chinese small and medium enterprises (SME) are accelerating expansion into Southeast Asia through low-cost digital strategies as war and shifting supply chains push firms to diversify beyond their home market, according to OCBC Bank (Hong Kong) Ltd.

OCBC is positioning its Hong Kong and Singapore network to capture rising cross-border activity as mainland Chinese and Hong Kong firms expand into ASEAN markets including Indonesia, Vietnam, Thailand and Malaysia.

“The key trend is they will build brands targeting overseas middle-class customers and leverage e-commerce platforms for quicker market entry,” Mimi Tsang, head of commercial banking cash, emerging business at OCBC Bank, told Asian Banking & Finance.

Consumer goods, digital solutions, logistics and environmental, social and governance-related businesses are among the sectors driving outbound expansion, she added.

China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology in April rolled out measures identifying “quality” SMEs and encouraged local governments to support overseas expansion through financing, tax, and industrial policies, according to state-owned news agency Xinhua.

“We see our clients using Hong Kong for capital structuring and treasuries, whilst Singapore serves as their ASEAN operation hub,” Tsang said via Zoom.

She said firms continue to face financing, compliance, and operational challenges even with digital-first expansion models. One issue that SMEs often face when expanding overseas is lack of financing, she pointed out.

OCBC’s regional network spans 250 branches across Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and Vietnam, giving SMEs local banking access without rebuilding relationships in each market.

Tsang said SMEs are also increasingly seeking support beyond financing, including tax, legal, and compliance guidance as they navigate unfamiliar regulatory environments and fragmented supply chains.

The rapid growth in young populations and the middle class will also push SMEs to go global, Tsang said.

OCBC earlier revealed plans to more than double its support for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) through sustainable financing.

The Singapore-headquartered bank aims to support 12,000 SMEs across Singapore, Malaysia, Hong Kong and Indonesia by 2028, up from just 5,000 in 2025, it said in an April announcement.

Commitments will include social loans as well as dedicated programmes to women entrepreneurs and women-led businesses in the four markets.

OCBC expects this move to drive its SME sustainable finance commitments from nearly $10.14b (S$13b) to $19.5b (S$25b) by 2028.

Sectors that drove the growth included building and construction, manufacturing, and transport and logistics.

Banks require CMA (Credit Monitoring Arrangement) data before approving working capital or term loans.

→ Balance sheet analysis
→ Working capital assessment

✔ Cash flow forecasts
✔ Projected balance sheet
✔ Assumption-based growth models

DSCR (Debt Service Coverage Ratio)

Banks want confidence that the business generates enough income to repay debt comfortably.

❌ Low DSCR = high rejection risk
✔ Strong DSCR = stronger approval probability

Many business owners spend decades building wealth…
but very few spend enough time planning how to protect it for their families.

The reality is — business comes with risk.

Over the past few years alone, we have seen:
• COVID-19 disrupt entire industries
• Rising interest rates and inflation
• Supply chain challenges
• Global geopolitical tensions including the Iran-Israel conflict
• Economic uncertainty affecting SMEs and cash flow worldwide

Even strong and established businesses can face unexpected financial pressure.

According to Malaysia’s Insolvency Department and related reports:
• Malaysia recorded thousands of bankruptcy cases annually post-pandemic
• Individuals aged 35–44 formed the largest bankruptcy group between 2020–2024 (Sinar Daily)
• Business loans remain among the major contributors to insolvency cases (Sinar Daily)
• Over 5,000 youths below age 34 were declared bankrupt from 2020 onwards (The Star)

This is why proper wealth structuring, succession planning and asset protection matter.

Living trusts and properly structured policy arrangements may help families create clearer separation and continuity planning — particularly when done early, transparently and in good faith.

As highlighted in legal and insolvency discussions:
✔ timing matters
✔ intent matters
✔ proper documentation matters

Structures created genuinely for succession, family protection and long-term planning are very different from last-minute arrangements intended to avoid creditors.

Many business owners focus heavily on:
✔ growing assets
✔ expanding businesses
✔ increasing revenue

…but neglect:
❌ estate planning
❌ liquidity planning
❌ succession arrangements
❌ family financial continuity

The question is not whether risk exists.
The question is whether your family is prepared if something unexpected happens.

We cannot predict the future — but we can prepare for it wisely.

If you are a business owner, entrepreneur or professional, this is a conversation worth having early, not during a crisis.

Legacy Advisor.

(Valuation) Boss, RM5 Million Sales Does Not Mean Your Company Is Worth RM5 Million

Last week, I asked one SME boss a simple question.
“Boss, how much do you think your company is worth?”

He answered very confidently.

“Mr Koh, last year sales RM5 million. So company value should be around RM5million lah.”

I smiled. This is where many SME bosses get valuation wrong.

Sales RM5million does not mean company value RM5 million.

A buyer does not pay you because your sales look big.
A buyer pays for profit.
A buyer pays for cash flow.
A buyer pays for systems.
A buyer pays for customers that can stay.
A buyer pays for a business that can still run after the boss walks out.

This is the painful part.

To the boss, the company is his baby.
30 years of hard work.
Sunday also work.
Public holiday also answer customer call.
Bank loan, supplier pressure, staff problem, customer problem, IRB letter, everything also he handles.

So when someone says the company may not be worth what he thinks, he feels hurt.

But valuation is not based on feeling.

A company with RM5 million sales but only 2% net margin may be less attractive than a smaller company with RM3 million sales and strong recurring profit.

Revenue is nice for storytelling.
Profit is nicer for valuation.
Cash flow is even nicer.
And clean documentation is the most beautiful.

Many SME bosses also think audited accounts already equal valuation.
No.
Audited accounts answer one question : “Are the financial statements fairly presented?”

Valuation asks another question : “What will a serious buyer actually pay for this business?”

Very different question.
Because a buyer will ask:

Are the profits sustainable?
Are customers too dependent on the founder?
Are personal expenses mixed inside the company?
Are directors’ salaries at market rate?
Are related party transactions properly recorded?
Can the business continue without the boss sitting in office every day?

If the answer is no, the value will be discounted.
Sometimes very heavily.

Now valuation is no longer only for selling business.
It matters for Capital Gains Tax on unlisted shares.
It matters for stamp duty on share transfers.
It matters for succession planning.
It matters when shareholders want to exit.
It matters when family business passes to the next generation.
It matters when IRB asks, “How did you arrive at this value?”

The biggest mistake?

Many SME owners only think about valuation when someone wants to buy their company.

By then, too late already.

Value is built years before the sale.
Clean accounts.
Less boss dependency.
Better margins.
Good systems.
Clear documents.
Proper governance.

All these boring things make buyers pay better.

So boss, don’t wait until someone offers you a low price, then only get angry and say : “Why my business so cheap?”

PS : Authored by Mr Koh Teck Peng, Chartered Accountant, Malaysia and Member of IACV (International Association of Certified Valuators).

KEEPING FINANCIAL RECORDS CAN IMPROVE YOUR CHANCES OF GETTING A LOAN

A business owner once walked into our office seeking a loan to expand her business. She was confident. Her shop was busy. Customers came in regularly. Sales appeared strong, and from her explanation, the business seemed profitable.

When the loan assessment process began, she was asked a simple question:

"Can you show us your sales records, expenses, and cash flow for the past few months?"

She paused. Her response was one I've heard many times:

"Everything is in my head."

The challenge was not that she lacked business experience. The challenge was that there was little documented evidence to support the figures she provided.

A few weeks later, another business owner applied for a similar facility. His business was smaller, but he arrived with a notebook containing daily sales records, expense tracking, inventory details, and account statements. The difference was clear.

One applicant relied on memory.

The other relied on records.

For lenders, records provide confidence. They help answer important questions:

✔️ How much does the business actually earn?

✔️ What are the regular expenses?

✔️ Is the cash flow sufficient to support loan repayment?

✔️ Is the business growing or struggling?

Without proper records, even a profitable business may find it difficult to demonstrate its true financial strength.

One of the most valuable habits any entrepreneur can develop is keeping accurate financial records. You don't need complicated accounting software to start.

A simple notebook, spreadsheet, or daily record book can make a significant difference.

Remember:

Good financial records don't just help you understand your business; they help others trust your business too. And in lending, trust is often the foundation of approval.

Do you currently keep records of your income and expenses, or do you rely mostly on memory?

(Tax Update) Boss, you think Tax Appeal is "Argue first, Talk reason"? 

Most of the time,
you pay first,
then slowly talk reason.

Uncle Chen walked into my office last month, face pale pale one.
Hand holding one LHDN assessment notice. Form JA.
Amount: RM380,000.

He sit down, straight away bang the table:
"I don't agree! I want to appeal!"

I looked at him, asked one question:
"Can. You want to appeal, no problem."
"But this RM380,000,
you know you may still need to pay first or not?"

He went quiet.
Just now the fire,
suddenly turned into cold sweat.

Because many SME bosses think,
tax dispute is like this:
I don't agree.
I appeal.
We sit down and talk.
Wait for the result, then only pay.
Reality is not like that one.

Under Malaysia tax system,
once the assessment notice Form JA is issued,
the tax usually must be paid within the period stated in the notice.
Appeal, doesn't mean automatic stop paying ah.

In English they call it :
Pay First, Appeal Later.

In Chinese, more straight:
先给钱, 再讲道理.

Sounds very harsh hor.
But this is the reality of Section 103 of the Income Tax Act.

The government's stand (past, present, and future) is very clear.

If everybody receive assessment then appeal,
then don't pay tax,
how is the country supposed to collect revenue?

So the rule is:
You can argue.
You can appeal.
You can talk reason.
But the money,
most of the time, you must arrange first.

This is where SME bosses suffer the most.
Not whether you have a case or not.

It's whether your cashflow can tahan,
until you finish talking your reason.

More realistic part is,
tax appeal is not today appeal,
tomorrow SCIT open court,
next month got result.
The cases are queuing,
maybe not a few months.
Maybe a few years.

Your money already paid.
Your case still queuing.
Your company still need to pay salary.
Suppliers still need to settle.
Bank loan still need to service.
Customers maybe still drag and drag.

At this point, tax dispute is not just a legal problem already.

It's a cashflow problem.
It's a "business live or die" problem.

Many bosses ask me:
"So I am very jialat lah?"

I usually say:
"Jialat or not, depends on whether you prepare ahead or not."

KTP gives SME bosses three simple reminders:

First, treat tax dispute as a cashflow event.
When the assessment notice come, don't only think:
"Who can help me argue?"

You also must immediately think:
"If really need to pay first, where this money coming from?"

Second, before the deadline, go and talk to LHDN.

Don't wait until last minute.

If the company really got cashflow problem,
you can try to apply for instalment or extension.

But you must take the first step.
You also must prepare proper financial documents,
show them you are not purposely dragging.

Third, your documents must be in order from day one.

I'm just the marketing guy here at Inflow Finance, and as I sit in the office and overhear client conversations, I can see the significant capacity we have to understand the nuances of every funding request. Big or small, we take the time to understand the client's strategy and situation without prejudice or judgment, but with a genuine desire to help facilitate a positive outcome.

Three SMEs were declined refinancing last quarter — not because of current performance, but because of credit events from 2021.

When does a borrower's past stop defining their future?

The conversation around credit history in Nigeria often focuses on punishment for default. But what we rarely discuss at the policy level is the pathway back.

A credit bureau system that only records failure without providing structured rehabilitation does two things: it creates a permanent underclass of excluded enterprises, and it reduces the total pool of bankable businesses in an economy that desperately needs growth.

Here's what concerns me most.

The current system assumes that time alone heals credit wounds. But SMEs operating in our macroeconomic environment face shocks that are often systemic — forex volatility, input cost inflation, or supply chain disruptions that have nothing to do with management competence.

Yet their credit records treat all defaults as equal moral failures.

Progressive credit history frameworks in other markets include provisions for: graduated rehabilitation timelines based on debt clearance milestones, distinctions between economic-driven and willful defaults, and formal mechanisms for rebuilding creditworthiness through supervised lending windows.

We need these conversations at the regulatory table.

The Central Bank's guidelines on credit reporting are comprehensive on capture and retention. But they're almost silent on restoration and reintegration.

This isn't just about fairness. It's about economic efficiency.

Every viable business locked out of formal finance either migrates to predatory informal channels or shuts down entirely. Both outcomes shrink our tax base, reduce employment, and weaken the financial system's reach.

If we're serious about deepening financial inclusion and supporting Nigeria's real economy, we need credit systems that are designed for resilience, not just compliance.

To regulators and policy architects working on credit infrastructure reform: let's explore what graduated credit rehabilitation could look like in our context. My DMs are open for structured conversations.
